title: Is USA Rare Earth Stock a Buy Now?

As of this writing on Nov. 19, the S&P 500 is tanking; indeed, the index is on track to notch its sixth consecutive day of losses. A few days ago, Nvidia's blockbuster earnings came and went without confetti -- or former CEO Jensen Huang. Widespread apprehension seems to pervade every nook and cranny of the stock market, as the uncertain future of artificial intelligence (AI) hangs over everything.

So what about mining stocks? What about rare-earths? We still need critical minerals. Could USA Rare Earth (NASDAQ:USAR) be the right stock to put your money in right now?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

USA Rare Earth generates revenue, but profits are a distant future

USA Rare Earth is a rare-earth mining company that wants to become a mine-to-magnet company. Its flagship mining project -- the Round Top deposit in Texas -- is currently under development, but its recent acquisition of the Brazilian mine Serra Verde means that USA Rare Earth is now an actual miner.

Production at Serra Verde began in 2024, and in October 2026, the mine began shipping rare-earth materials to a U.S. government-backed buyer under a 15-year purchasing agreement.

Image source: Getty Images.

Those shipments have given USA Rare Earth something that many early-stage miners need badly: revenue. Still, it's nothing to write home about. Last quarter, USA Rare Earth generated about $3 million, notably missing Wall Street's expectations of $6.5 million. Worse, it reported an operating loss of about $141 million and an adjusted loss of $0.44 per share, more than double the $0.19 loss analysts expected.

So, is USA Rare Earth stock a buy?

In today's market, with several macroeconomic headwinds blowing together, I want to encourage a cautious approach to USA Rare Earth.

There's no question in my mind that rare-earth metals will be valuable in the future. We have plenty of uses for them, and their scarcity has many governments concerned. But that doesn't mean every rare-earth mining company will be a winner on Wall Street, and for USA Rare Earth, two risks need to be considered.

The first is that Round Top Deposit, its flagship project, is still in the exploration phase: Its commercial viability has not been determined. Even more concerning is the fact that miners have been trying to develop Round Top for decades without commercial success. Its history stretches back to the 1970s, when it was investigated for fluorite, and the asset has changed hands several times before coming under USA Rare Earth's control.

These are interesting times, with Congressional upheaval in the United States amid an uncertain economic environment with rising interest rates, elevated inflation, and potentially slowing economic growth.

It is typically not a great combination for most financial sector stocks, as the sector often serves as an economic bellwether and thrives when the economy is strong. The S&P 500 financials sector has returned just 2.7% year-to-date, which is among the worst performers among sectors.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Many financial stocks have tumbled in recent weeks, caught up in the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 sell-off over the past month. Here are two financial stocks that are at or near 52-week lows that are good long-term buys, even amid the lackluster outlook for the sector in 2027.

Image source: Getty Images.

1. Nu Holdings

Nu Holdings (NYSE:NU) is the parent company of Nubank, a Brazil-based bank and financial firm. Nu stock is down 28% year-to-date, but most of that has come in the past month, when the stock has plummeted 17% to its current $11.95 per share, which is hovering near a 52-week low.

The reason for the swoon is almost entirely due to the results of the presidential election in October, where the liberal incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva beat the conservative challenger Flavio Bolsonaro in a surprise victory.

Most Brazilian stocks tanked after the Lula victory, as the challenger was seen as a better option to spur Brazil's economic growth. But Lula has been in office for three terms already, a time when Nu has been growing like a weed, so it seems like more of a knee-jerk reaction than anything to do with Nu's business model or prospects.

For investors, it is a tremendous opportunity to buy the dip on this valuation reset. Nu stock is trading at just 11 times forward earnings and has a minuscule five-year P/E-to-growth (PEG) ratio of 0.13, suggesting it is well undervalued relative to its long-term earnings.

While Nu is the largest bank in Brazil, the low-overhead digital bank has expanded into Mexico and Colombia. And in September, it launched in the United States. Its growth has been impressive, as in the most recent quarter, revenue rose 37% year over year to a record $6.3 billion, gross profit jumped 35% to $2.6 billion, and net income climbed 31% to a record $1.1 billion.

title: Micron Stock Just Hit Its Lowest Price Since May. I'd Buy More Now.

Micron Stock Just Hit Its Lowest Price Since May. I'd Buy More Now.

Shares of Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) fell about 14% on Friday to close near $595. That's the lowest close for the memory chipmaker's stock since early May.

Micron closed at a record high of $1,213.56 on June 25, so the stock has lost about half its value over five months. And memory stocks dropped across the board on Friday, with Sandisk down about 16%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

But management said in late September that customers had already committed to over three-quarters of Micron's planned shipments for this fiscal year. At roughly $595, the stock costs about 3.5 times expected earnings for that year, fiscal 2027, which ends in early September 2027.

I think the fall has more to do with worries over memory prices than with how much Micron can sell.

Image source: Getty Images.

Customers have claimed most of this year's chips

Micron president and chief operating officer Manish Bhatia said on the company's Sept. 30 earnings call that "we have more than 75% of our shipments committed for the year," referring to fiscal 2027. He added that this "allows us to shift our conversations on allocation with our customers out to 2028."

Put another way, buyers have mostly claimed their share of Micron's output through next September, and the talks have already moved on.

The numbers back that up, helped by demand from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. Micron's revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter, the 14 weeks ending Sept. 3, came to $54.2 billion. That was 31% higher than in the previous quarter and 379% above the year-ago quarter. Earnings per share climbed more than elevenfold year over year, to $32.87. For the first quarter of fiscal 2027, management sees revenue of about $61.5 billion, roughly 13% above fiscal Q4, and it expects every quarter of the year to beat the one before.

So growth is easing from a blistering pace. But it isn't reversing.

Prices are the bigger risk

Committed shipments, though, don't all come with committed prices. Micron's multiyear strategic customer agreements, which it estimates will make up over 35% of its revenue through 2030, are where it sets most prices ahead of time. Even in those deals, around a quarter of the expected revenue is priced periodically based on market prices.

That probably leaves most of Micron's sales linked to where memory prices head. And prices did a lot of the work last quarter.

title: Meet the Warren Buffett Rule That Makes This Consumer Stock a Buy With $1,000 Right Now
detail:
Meet the Warren Buffett Rule That Makes This Consumer Stock a Buy With $1,000 Right Now
Micah Zimmerman, The Motley Fool

Shortly after buying Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRKB)(NYSE:BRKA), Warren Buffett picked up a Baltimore department store because it looked like a bargain. Three years later, he wrote that he "was lucky to sell the business for about what I had paid." His lesson became one of his most quoted lines: "It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price."

I keep coming back to that rule, because one of my favorite unglamorous retailers finally has a fair price.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

A wonderful company having a lousy year

Tractor Supply (NASDAQ:TSCO) sells what rural life runs on: animal feed, pet food, fencing, and tools. It's the largest rural lifestyle retailer in the U.S., with nearly 2,500 stores.

This year has been bumpy. A rough May dragged down the second quarter, and the company cut its outlook in July. Bigger purchases remain soft, and CEO Hal Lawton said, "Elevated interest rates and reduced housing mobility are weighing on property improvements and larger projects."

The everyday stuff held up, though. Consumables like animal feed and bedding beat the store average, and same-store sales went from negative in July to growing by September. Neighbor's Club loyalty members made up nearly 82% of sales, and CFO Kurt Barton put it plainly: "Tractor Supply remains a differentiated business with significant competitive advantages." A crowd that loyal is my kind of economic moat.

New ways to reach the farm gate

Management isn't waiting around. It used tariff refunds to cut prices on about 50 everyday essentials, raised its Freshpet cooler rollout to about 1,000 stores, and now has its Allivet pharmacy filling prescriptions for VIP Petcare, the mobile vet business it bought. On Nov. 12, it joined the platform of Uber Technologies, so shoppers can get dog food or garden supplies delivered. "The need for convenience doesn't stop at the city limits," said Uber retail executive Nathan Bernheim, while Tractor Supply digital chief Matthew Rubin noted that "millions of Uber users have a new way to discover Tractor Supply."

Not every bet paid off. The company closed 74 money-losing Petsense pet stores last quarter, and higher fuel and freight costs squeezed margins.

Shopify (NASDAQ:SHOP) is a fast-growing e-commerce powerhouse with tons of opportunity ahead. It looks like a fantastic opportunity for investors in every way except one, but that one is quite important: It has an extremely rich price tag.

What will happen in 10 years?

Shopify has become a major player in e-commerce. It doesn't rank with the top e-commerce retailers because it doesn't sell anything online; it sells services, from full websites to point-of-sale devices for omnichannel clients, for e-commerce retailers.

But its gross merchandise volume, or the total sales of its clients, was $119 billion in the third quarter, which is more than Amazon's (NASDAQ:AMZN) online and third-party sales of $116 billion.

Revenue increased 32% year over year in the third quarter, impressive in this sticky-inflation environment, and it reported a 22% cash flow margin.

Shopify is a great company, but it's expensive on just about every valuation metric.

That makes me hesitant to recommend it as a strong buy. You might imagine that in 10 years it's bound to reward shareholders, but that's not necessarily the case.

Consider PayPal Holdings (NASDAQ:PYPL), a Shopify competitor in certain services. Ten years ago, it was the pioneer in digital payments, but it has gained a grand total of 53% over the past decade after losing ground.

I think Shopify is a great stock to hold for the next 10 years, but I'd wait for a better entry point.

Wall Street expects the following top growth stocks to deliver 19% or better annual earnings growth, putting a double by 2031 within reach.

Amazon

Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN)shares closed at $257.89 on Nov. 17, up 11% over the past year and 45% over the past five years, trailing the S&P 500's 56% five-year return. The reason it can double by 2031 is expanding margins, which the market hasn't fully priced in yet.

Over the past three years, Amazon's trailing-12-month operating income has risen 283% to $106 billion. Amazon's most profitable business is its cloud services segment. Still, it has many levers to increase profitability from growth in other non-retail services, which make up the majority of its $797 billion in annual revenue.

Advertising is a profitable business to watch. Amazon sells ads to brands and sellers that want to reach its shoppers. Ad revenue grew 12% year over year on a constant-currency basis to $19.6 billion in the third quarter, bringing it close to $80 billion annually.

However, that growth doesn't show the real momentum. Moving Prime Day into Q2 cut 8.5 percentage points from Q3 ad growth, according to CEO Andy Jassy. Excluding currency swings, ad sales grew 22% to 26% in each of the five prior quarters, and management expects ad growth to return to the high teens in Q4.

Amazon trades at about 27 times forward earnings, which is reasonable given analysts' expectations that earnings will grow about 24% per year over the coming years. If the valuation multiple holds, and Amazon delivers on those expectations, the stock could more than double by 2031.

Airbnb

Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB)shares closed at $180.94 on Nov. 17, up 54% over the past year but down 9% over the past five years. The business has continued to grow, creating a good buying opportunity.

Management says "Airbnb is back in growth mode." Q3 revenue rose 19% year over year, its fastest growth in more than three years, and management raised its full-year outlook.

Vistra (NYSE:VST) stock was swept up in the artificial intelligence (AI) sell-off in November, but its decline began well before this month's midterm elections. Power producers have faced regulatory scrutiny over rising consumer electricity prices and who foots the bill for data centers' growing energy demands.

With the market weighing the AI data center build-out narrative, Vistra's beaten-down stock is worth buying the dip on before November ends. Here's why.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Vistra has had a tough year as regulators scrutinize deals

After a strong performance in 2025, Vistra stock has fallen 20% this year. Regulators across major data center hubs have pushed back on electricity deals to ensure ratepayers don't end up paying for higher costs and grid expansions.

Midterm election results, notably in Texas, cast a shadow over the ongoing data center build-out. That said, outgoing Governor Greg Abbott had already paused permits and ERCOT approvals while the grid operator audited grid impacts. Not only that, but evolving rules requiring data centers to bring their own energy favor Vistra, which is contracting directly with hyperscalers while adding capacity.

Vistra has reached agreements with Meta Platforms and Amazon Web Services, and under these power purchase agreements, the hyperscalers are funding capacity uprates, addressing one of the biggest concerns while Vistra locks in long-term cash flow.

Here's why Vistra stock is a buy in November

Management forecasts adjusted EBITDA of $7.7 billion to $8.5 billion, and most of its 2027 capacity is already hedged, protecting near-term cash flows. The stock is down, and Vistra's management announced it would add another $1.5 billion to its share repurchase program, capitalizing on the beaten-down stock.

For investors bullish on long-term power demand from data centers, Vistra stock is quite appealing at today's price, now trading at just 13 times its forecasted 2027 earnings.
